New on our Science Blog: How AI is beginning to change scientific modeling.

Scientific models help researchers explain
items.content:
New on our Science Blog: How AI is beginning to change scientific modeling.

Scientific models help researchers explain and predict real-world systems—like how a single nerve cell fires, or what happens when neutron stars collide. Recent advances have transformed how scientists fit complex models to data. But scientists still typically write the models manually, and usually need to weigh up several competing versions, each of which might explain the data in a different way.

In a guest post, Jakob Macke, Daniel Gedon, and Stefan Wahl describe how AI is starting to help with these parts of the process. By writing, running, fitting, and revising scientific models as code, AI can explore many possible model structures, and find out which explanations the data support.

HubSpot co-founder and CTO Dharmesh Shah says it's less scary to build an AI startup now than in 2023, as long as you stay off the Yellow Brick Road the frontier labs are following:

"The frontier model companies have invested hundreds of billions of dollars building, doing the pre-training. And so their whole business effectively now is taking the capex that they've spent and the money they're continuing to spend and saying, 'How do we sell inference? How do we sell tokens? How do we monetize the thing that we've built?'"

"There are SaaS companies and startups that know their particular domain, know their market, have some distribution, or have something that allows them to sell tokens and be a reseller of inference."

"Think of AI as infrastructure in the same way we thought of AWS and cloud infrastructure 15 years ago... I think it's less scary now to build in and around the AI arena than it was in 2023."

"We have open source. We have lots of great commercial products. So as long as you stay off the Yellow Brick Road, it is completely possible now that you're not gonna get margined out, because you have options."

@dharmesh

items.content:
Former Cisco M&A head Mike Volpi on why he’s more optimistic about AI than the dot-com era: the internet built communication, AI is building intelligence.

Guido Appenzeller: “Is there one other big difference from how it was back then, which is that everything is now much, much larger? Back then we were investing a small fraction of a percent in infrastructure for the internet. Today we’re investing 2% or so of our GDP in AI infrastructure.”

Mike: “It is much bigger, but in the 100,000 feet abstraction, what is it that is being built? Back then it was communication that was being built. Today we’re building intelligence. And the economic value of intelligence is probably higher than the economic value of communication.”

“I also think that, believe it or not, it’s been nearly 30 years, the markets are more efficient now, which is why so much more risk capital is willing to make its way into AI.”

“So net is, I’m actually more optimistic about this cycle, but I also believe that there will be some correction and some cleaning up of the industry structure.”

items.content:
Huge AI announcements from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI right now:

1. The authors of AI 2027 just moved their timelines up. They now expect AI on par with the best human AI researchers to arrive in 2027, after METR estimated Anthropic is improving about 2x as fast thanks to AI. Daniel Kokotajlo gives it a 50-50 chance by May 2027 and says he's "scared, sad, and angry." 

2. Anthropic opened the investor pitch for its IPO, with shares likely trading as soon as Thursday next week. An updated filing also says it has now crossed its own safety line for AI-driven progress. 

3. OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT, a beta hub where brands can set up AI agents for shoppers, claim a verified profile, and track how often ChatGPT mentions them. Paid ads can point users to those agents too. This is like the start of SEO for chatbots.

4. Anthropic rolled out Claude Sheets and Whiteboards in beta, made Claude Data generally available, and announced Claude Meetings, an assistant that sits in on your video calls. Add those to Slides, Design, and Docs. Seems like Claude is slowly rebuilding the entire office suite.

5. Anthropic also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 yesterday, with Fable debuting at #1 on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, 5 points ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon. It's also 20% cheaper and up to 30% faster than 5.1. Google lost the top spot before Carbon even shipped (!)

6. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for high-volume agent work. It ties Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Intelligence Index at roughly one-third of the cost per task ($0.14 vs. $0.41 on an average test). Meta shipped its first Muse model in April and now has an answer for every tier OpenAI and Anthropic sell.

7. Google announced 2 new AI chips coming next year: the TPU 8tx, which keeps data encrypted even while a model is working on it, and the 8i Max, which joins 2 chips into one for agents that need to hold an entire codebase in view. Google already has nearly 100 TPU customers (including Anthropic and Apple) and every available chip is spoken for. 

8. Nvidia's top lawyer reportedly emailed agents in August 2025 while they were investigating whether Singapore's Megaspeed smuggled its chips to China. The Commerce Department then halted the case and handed it to the Justice Department. Not a great week for Nvidia.

9. Adobe signed a multi-year deal with Disney to build custom AI models trained on Disney's characters and visual styles, with work already underway for theme parks, film, and ESPN. Pretty interesting to see one of the most protective IP owners in entertainment is now training its own AI models.

10. OpenAI acquired Odessia, a months-old AI trip-planning startup from Sonder founder Francis Davidson, who is joining OpenAI to work on travel. Between this and #3, ChatGPT is coming for shopping and travel.

11. France unveiled the Paris Call for AI Safety and Security, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral committing to build emergency off switches into their most advanced models. Interesting timing given #1 on this list.

Daily reminder that this is the worst AI will ever be.

Everything I do with AI is in an effort to reach this north star

items.content:
I'm gonna try to keep this post to 57 seconds read, but these are the Claude tips you cannot afford to ignore:

1. Use the Claude desktop app (even after Cowork is gone)

Not 'Claude in browser'. The day you start using the app, you'd be able to work with your folders without ever uploading the files. You'd use Claude code more. Trust me, there is no coming back from there.

2. Always reach out for Opus 5.5 (not Fable 5.2)

Default should be: Opus 5.5 on high. Fable 5.2 is insanely good but burns your token in just 3-4 prompts. You won't be able to complete any task with Fable 5.2. 

3. Do not switch the Claude models mid-chat. 

It consumes more tokens because Claude re-reads the entire chat (again) to get the context.

4. Delete your old Claude setup.

Delete the “Instructions for Claude” box in settings. Delete the old added Claude skills. Old skills and prompts might be slowing you down since they were written for old models. Instead, give one goal & end prompts with: “Before you start, restate my goal in your own words.”

5. Turn your Claude Memory ON.

Claude team tested it with & without memory. With memory, Opus 5.5 scored 28% better. Just, click “+” in chat box → turn on 'Memory'.

6. But keep your memory short.

Claude had 105 facts about me before starting a session, but after one prompt, it came down to 26. To copy my exact prompt to clean memory, go to https://t.co/U9NLc2FuiR

7. Ask for HTML. Not for a document.

Add two things to your prompt: “Make it an HTML page” and “for [who will read it].”

Claude will code the image, doc, or any other format. There is no scope of making mistakes.

8. Never argue with Claude. It is pointless.

You'll end up burning your tokens without finishing the task. Instead, click on “Edit” on your already sent prompt right before the bad answer. Change, edit, or fix. Click “Save”.

9. Delete your instructions box.

Remove “about me”, “how I write” file, list of rules. They all force Claude to limit its creativity. Aim to give one clear goal per prompt.

10. One Claude Project per client.

Inside the project, turn off “Use account memory”. Now what Claude knows about Client A doesn't get mixed up with Client B.

11. Ask for the spread.

When Claude gives you the most generic answer (that’s literally how it works). Push it to give you the weird, unlikely ones. Use this prompt:

“Give me 20 very different options. For each one, tell me how likely another AI would give it to me. The last two must be under 10%.”

12. Give Claude a finish line.

Define what 'done' means to you, by using these:

“Done means: a one-page doc my boss can forward without editing.”

13. Above tips barely scratched the surface of mastering Claude. To go even deeper, get the other 11 tips + prompts from the same guide: https://t.co/U9NLc2FuiR

> Setting that stops Claude from downgrading.
> How one GitHub link becomes a skill.
> The only prompt you’ll ever need.
> What to do when Claude gets dumb.

items.content:
Stop saying AI doesn’t show judgment. 

Of course it shows judgment.

And actually, you already trust some of its judgment. 

When you ask it to find you an apartment and it goes on Zillow and not https://t.co/sUfKNrbqKz, that is judgment. 

When you ask it to make you a slideshow for a quick presentation to your boss on an extremely dense topic, it will only provide a few slides. That is judgment. 

When you’re replying to a question from a 7-year-old and their email is filled with emojis, and the AI writes like you but adds 1-2 emojis to better match the inbound email, that is judgment. 

Probabilistic models reasoning through infinite options toward a goal is “judgment”, though I’m not saying whether AI is literally judging - just that it is showing it. Researchers can weigh in on that nuance. 

Your personal judgment might be BETTER or WIDER, particularly if it’s in a field you are deeply familiar with, but let’s not pretend we don’t already partially rely on AI’s displayed judgment to get work done.

items.content:
Five non-coding methods I use to make my AI adversarial reviews more helpful:

1/ Multiple personas as subagents
I have Claude spin up three separate subagents, each one a different reviewer: someone who loves our product and uses it for everything, someone who hates our product and wants to destroy us, and someone who has no idea what’s going on and keeps making mistakes. In product reviews, you can combine this with your customer avatar reviews (ie descriptions of your 5 ideal buyers).

2/ Make the reviews multimodal
Ask AI to not only review the PRD or product as these personas, but also to record actual video walkthroughs as the persona, take screenshots, tweet fake tweets about it. It's not enough to just review in text format. Also ask them to review it multiple times. 

3/ Use all your subscriptions
Ask other AI systems to review it with those personas or to invent personas and do the same combo of steps one and two or just to review it for issues/bugs/errors. If you built it in Claude, have Codex review. If you built in Codex, have Antigravity review, etc.

4/ Multilayered judging
The main agent collects all the feedback from the personas and reviews the work itself. Pretty much everyone stops there. Gremlin mode: make the main agent pass it BACK to the subagents to review again, who then pass it BACK to the main agent to collate. Not enough people are playing AI as a judge or AI ping-pong as my team calls it. You can still ask for the full and complete list of feedback points and mark out which ones were added/removed at each switch. 

5/ Tell the AI it’s someone else’s work
This one is more anecdotal, but I find the review meaningfully improves when the AI thinks the work isn’t mine. So instead of “review this email draft,” try “review this email draft - it’s written by my cousin who always says the wrong thing.” Or instead of “review this app and make it better,” try “hey review this app - my best friend made it and more than anything, even if it means disappointing her in the short-term, I want her to succeed.”

Years ago, when Anthropic first rolled out Claude, they told the world they wanted Claude to be the three Hs: helpful, honest, and harmless. I believe OpenAI had essentially the same three, just with synonyms.

My theory for the fifth tip above centers on “helpful.” When it’s my work, helpful immediately translates to compliment me. Model sycophancy is poison for outcomes imo, though it has certainly gotten better over time.

Take your name off your work (temporarily).

Then loop it again.

items.title: Launch HN: Pomerado (YC F26) – Turn any website into an MCP for agents
items.content:
Launch HN: Pomerado (YC F26) – Turn any website into an MCP for agents Hi HN, we’re Alan and Akshay from Pomerado (https://pomerado.ai/). We connect your agents to any website by turning sites into deterministic, self-healing APIs in minutes, fully self-serve.

Agents are no longer limited by their intelligence, but rather by their ability to interact with systems. Airlines, banks, e-commerce, insurance portals, government sites, and legacy portals all lack APIs or MCPs and are common parts of personal assistant or business workflows. Agents instead rely on browser automation or computer use, which can be slow, expensive, and unreliable. And even if computer use were perfect, most companies have banned it out of security and compliance concerns.

We discovered this problem while tinkering with our own personal assistants. When OpenClaw came out, we wanted to “live our lives through our agents” and have them do everything for us. We soon found their usefulness was restricted by what tools they could connect to. For example, when trying to book flights, they fell back on computer use, which failed to checkout. These issues got magnified on repeated workflows, like searching many airlines at once.

Pomerado started off as a project to improve these personal assistant workflows. As we started building, we realized that just-in-time tool creation could have significant applications for AI builders in legacy verticals.

We’re ex-McKinsey and Scale AI, where we drove agent deployments in healthcare, professional services, and telecom. Each time, the biggest bottleneck was getting agents to interface well with legacy websites and apps.

Pomerado is what we built. It’s a self-serve platform where devs can create APIs for any website (even those they don’t own), in minutes. Users (or their coding agents) provide a short natural language description, answer a few questions about their workflow, and receive a MCP in less than an hour. Future tool calls use the deterministic MCP, which usually returns results in 5-30 seconds.

Here’s a walkthrough of our product: https://youtu.be/Bi4jci7rgHo

In practice:

- Our agent opens a browser, explores the website, and performs the requested task once by writing HTTP requests or a Playwright script. This example run establishes how to navigate the website, interact with the relevant controls, and obtain the desired result. If any additional user input is needed (e.g., login, clarification) the agent will ask the user over MCP.

- Afterwards, the agent uses the example run, along with all of the data it recorded, to create a generalizable and repeatable API. Throughout this process, a separate Guardian model reviews the coding agent’s calls against a set of guardrails. We also run a battery of tests with synthetic inputs to ensure that the API is generalized and not overfit to one input. A final publication agent ensures that the integration publishes a reasonable and generalized input/output schema

- We also handle sites that require authentication and 2FA. For authentication, we pass off to a deterministic sign-in process to ensure the model and our recorders never read customer credentials. Users can store 2FA TOTP seeds or link their account to a Pomerado phone number for us to autofill 2FA for them as well

- If future runs fail, a maintenance job is kicked off to repair and improve the tool. The maintenance job can fix broken steps (e.g., a renamed button), add additional functionality (e.g., searching for business class flights in addition to economy), or add new guardrails (e.g., reservation dates must be in the future). We’ve even seen people improve tools by just saying “please make this faster”

Unlike computer use, our MCPs are deterministic at runtime, which makes them much faster and cheaper. By taking slightly longer to do a task the first time, you reap the benefits much more in the future. It’s a great fit for repeated, high-volume tasks you want your agent to do.

We’d love to have you try it! We have both an open-source (MIT) (https://github.com/Pomerado/pomerado) and a free hosted version (https://app.pomerado.ai).

So far, users of Pomerado include:

- A personal trainer using agents to prepare workouts and message clients. Before Pomerado, agents couldn’t login and use the site reliably, so this was all manual

- Car dealerships connecting their Grok Bots to legacy dealer systems, including marketplaces, CRMs, and ERPs. Dealers switched from computer use, which could take 1hr+

- Personal assistants using Pomerado to integrate with a broad range of consumer websites

Please ask any questions or share any feedback in the comments, thanks!

items.title: Show HN: Klad, a paint app your coding agent can drive (source-available)
items.content:
Show HN: Klad, a paint app your coding agent can drive (source-available) I've been developing applications for a long time and have turned to game development as well lately. One of the things that frustrated me the most was that using AI agents for game development is very annoying in the art department. Your only options right now are to either use an image genAI model and roll the dice every time you want to make an edit, or have your agent draw with something like vectors.

I was looking for an application that would allow me to ask an agent to make a first draft of whatever art I needed with actual brushes, and then be able to go in myself and edit every last stroke or layer that it created.

Klad is that application. Written in Rust, it can be fully controlled by an agent through the CLI, and every function is available in a nice UI as well: a brush engine, frame-by-frame animation (and bones/IK), vectors, text layers, colours, layer effects, infinite undo (even after re-opening the file!),…

Why I think it's useful for a wider audience: Adobe showed agents editing Photoshop files at MAX this week, with a private beta planned for early 2027.

Klad is built on the same core idea, with editable paint strokes as core architecture, and it works today.

Clone the repo to try it out: https://github.com/klad-app/klad

You can basically point Claude to the repo, ask it to build it, and pick up the drawing skills. Then ask it to make any drawing you want! (After that, you or the agent can change absolutely every brush stroke in the app again, which makes edits a breeze.)

The quality of the drawings really depends on the agent you use. I have tried it with Claude Fable 5.2 since it came out on Monday, and the drawings are already quite impressive. I'm confident that this will only improve.

I use it every day on Mac, so that definitely works well. It builds on Linux too (tablet pen pressure still needs some work there). Windows builds in CI, I haven't used it there myself yet but I have some reports that it works perfectly fine.

Coming up next is support for pixel art. I'm in the testing phase with this right now, and I expect it to go live in the repo sometime this weekend.

Klad is source-available rather than open source: free to build and use for individuals and small companies, and I plan to sell pre-built binaries later, the way Aseprite does. The file format, CLI reference and agent skill are MIT.

What I want to hear from people who try it: Can your agent work out the CLI without help, and where does it get confused? Can you go in and change one of its strokes easily?

The command reference and guides are available at https://klad.studio

I'll be here answering any questions about the technical side as well, as it's a pretty interesting challenge to build a performant engine with editable brush strokes that render as paint.

items.content:
Show HN: Aircad – Professional drafting and 3D modeling in the browser Aircad is a professional CAD system running in the browser with deep AI integration. It includes professional grade drafting and documentation tools, NURBS-based solid modeling, and a lot more. You can make professional quality design documents with it. It is all integrated behind a scripting API that can do anything you can do in the interface and also perform complex modeling operations efficiently. It reads and writes file formats like DXF, DWG, STEP, and 3DM.

I built Aircad because I was frustrated with what was out there. Current CAD tools are expensive and slow to improve. New features barely move the needle. With Aircad, you have fast, powerful geometry tools for just about anything, from conceptual models to your final design.

The newer generation of web-based CAD isn’t comprehensive enough to complete a project or is slower than existing desktop products because it sends performance-sensitive work to a server (OnShape), or isn’t designed to scale to real work in a collaborative setting (many "toy" CAD tools).

Current CAD collaboration workflows are fragile, costly, and complex. They’re file-based and separate the design artifacts (eg PDFs) from the source. Collaboration is often an expensive add-on that raises your subscription, is hard to learn, and feels unnatural. Aircad builds it in: version history, drawing comparison, forking, and realtime collaboration.

AI in most CAD tools is tacked on as a plug-in instead of being deeply integrated, and those plug-ins are often inefficient, hard to adopt, and costly. Aircad has a built-in AI agent and a comprehensive scripting API with a stage-and-commit workflow, so you know exactly what is happening during a complex change. You can use AI to write new scripts and commands that extend Aircad with repeatable, shareable workflows.

If you want to become dangerously good at Claude. You have to know which Claude tool to use, when (a few features were released yesterday):

1. Full guide + prompts at: https://t.co/psB7XxAv8w.
2. Don't pay anything. It's free in the email.
3. Send it to your team's Slack or group chat.

---

1. ASK → Chat
☑ Cowork has merged in Chat.
☑ For a quick question. Add “No web search & files”

2. THINK → Opus 5.5
☑ It won't burn that many tokens. Use it for all chat.
☑ Make it as your default model.

3. SPEED → Low effort
☑ For grammar, reformatting & translations.
☑ Lower effort for faster speed, never the model.

4. REASON → High effort
☑ For one-shot, super-ambitious work.
☑ Make it your default. Never Extra. Never Max.

5. DELEGATE → Auto mode
☑ Switch Manual to Auto. Your life will be better.
☑ Claude without your permission every second.

6. SHIP → Claude Code
☑ The Code tab in the Claude desktop app.
☑ Sites with GitHub + Vercel. Never coming back

7. FINISH → /goal command
☑ Tell Claude what “done” means.
☑ “/goal [task] until [result], or stop after 100 turns.”

8. SLIDES → Claude Design > Slides
☑ Claude Left bar > Design > Slides.
☑ Plan the outline in text first. Then: “Build this exact deck.” You can even give your brandkit.

9. MOCKUP → Claude Design
☑ Upload references. Prompt until you like it.
☑ Send a screenshot instead of describing.

10. ANIMATE → Claude Motion
☑ Type /motion in the chat.
☑ Say who watches, where & how long.
☑ Export to MP4.

11. ANALYZE → Claude Dashboards
☑ Attach a CSV or connect your data warehouse.
☑ Ask a question, not for a chart. Click any number.

12. RENDER → HTML Artifacts
☑ Prompt “Make it an HTML page.”
☑ Opens on your phone. Shared as a link.

13. BROWSE → Claude in Chrome
☑ Browsing agent to read any page.
☑ It can click on things, instead of just talking.

14. CLICK → Computer Use
☑ It clicks, types & works in your desktop apps.
☑ For native apps. Websites go through Chrome.

15. WRITE → Claude Docs (new)
☑ Claude Artifacts → Claude Docs.
☑ Use Claude Sheets, Data, and whiteboards.

15. SEARCH → Web Search
☑ Claude can decide when to search by itself.
☑ It reads the live web before answering.

16. INVESTIGATE → Research
☑ Type /deep-research or toggle it on the ‘+’.
☑ Don't use for one source, only when you need 20+ sources.

17. TRIGGER → Skills
☑ Go to Customize → Skills. Delete the old ones.
☑ Those skills are likely built for older models and can make answers worse.

Claude Code for GTM in 2026 is where Clay was in 2022, and the agencies waiting for a tutorial are the ones who'll miss it.

In 2022 you could learn Clay in a weekend, build tables nobody else had, and sell them as a service.

Clay's valuation went from $500M in June 2024 to $3.1B by August 2025.

Plenty of the GTM agencies running today were built inside that window.

Then everyone learned it.

The templates got shared, every client got the same table, and Clay's new pricing started charging for Actions on top of data credits.

We still use Clay every week, and so does every agency we compete with.

Claude Code is sitting where Clay sat in 2022.

A skill file and a context doc now do what used to take a table with 30 columns.

Our strategy skill runs 7 research steps off one URL:

> maps the market, segments the TAM and builds ICPs
> writes cold email scripts for every persona
> hands back the strategy as 3 client-ready PDFs

It puts the client's own sales call and onboarding form above anything it scrapes, so the strategy comes from what they said about themselves.

You want this running before every agency has it, so I'm giving away the full skill, all 7 prompts included.

A production-ready AI agent requires multiple technologies working together — from models and memory to tools, security, automation, and infrastructure.

Each layer plays a different role in making AI agents intelligent, reliable, and scalable.

Let's break down the 10 essential layers.

1. Models — The Intelligence Layer

The foundation of every AI agent.

LLMs understand instructions, reason through problems, and generate responses.

Popular options:

- OpenAI
- Claude
- Google Gemini
- Mistral AI
- Meta Llama

2. Agent Frameworks — Build Agent Systems

Examples:

- LangGraph
- CrewAI
- Microsoft AutoGen
- Agno
- AWS Strands Agents

3. Knowledge & RAG — Give Agents External Knowledge

RAG allows agents to retrieve relevant information from documents and external data sources before responding.

Popular tools:

- LangChain
- LlamaIndex
- Haystack
- DSPy
- GraphRAG

4. Memory & Context — Help Agents Remember

Memory allows agents to retain information from previous interactions and maintain context across tasks.

Tools include:

- Mem0
- Zep
- Letta
- Redis
- PostgreSQL

5. Tooling & MCP — Connect External Systems

MCP provides a standardized way for AI agents to connect with external tools, applications, and data sources.

Examples:

- MCP SDK
- FastMCP
- GitHub MCP Server
- Slack MCP Server
- Filesystem MCP Server

6. Security & Guardrails — Keep Agents Safe

Security layers control what agents can access and execute.

Popular solutions:

- NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails
- Guardrails AI
- Microsoft Presidio
- Lakera Guard
- Prompt Security

7. Observability & Evals — Monitor Performance

These tools help developers track agent behavior, evaluate outputs, identify errors, and improve reliability.

Examples:

- LangSmith
- Langfuse
- Arize Phoenix
- Weights & Biases
- TruLens

8. Automation & Workflows — Make Agents Productive

Automation tools connect different services and enable agents to execute multi-step workflows.

Popular options:

- n8n
- Zapier
- Make
- Microsoft Power Automate
- Temporal

9. Vector DB & Storage — Store and Retrieve Data

Vector databases help agents search and retrieve relevant information using semantic similarity.

Examples:

- Pinecone
- Weaviate
- Qdrant
- Milvus
- pgvector
- Elasticsearch

10. Infrastructure — Run Everything at Scale

Infrastructure provides the computing resources and deployment environment needed to run AI applications reliably.

Popular technologies:

- Docker
- Kubernetes
- AWS
- Google Cloud
- Microsoft Azure
- Terraform

items.content:
🛠️🧭 "How We Solved Agent Building" got me digging.

If you are building AI Agents for real business workflows, you have probably struggled with:

agent handoffs, lost context, complex orchestration, failed tool calls, and agents that work in demos but struggle with real user questions.

I watched a talk on AI Engineer about how Vercel tried several agent architectures before a simple file system beat their multi-agent system.

So I pulled together their 6 stages and the open-source tools worth exploring at each one.

Here are 19 GitHub repos worth knowing for AI Agent building in 2026:

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟭: 𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁

✸ Vercel AI SDK → unified model access  
✸ LiteLLM → multi-provider LLM gateway  
✸ Instructor → structured LLM outputs

→ Test whether the LLM can generate valid SQL.

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟮: 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺

✸ LangGraph → stateful agent orchestration  
✸ CrewAI → role-based agent collaboration  
✸ Google ADK → multi-agent conversations  
✸ OpenAI Agents SDK → agents + handoffs

→ Specialized agents, but context gets lost in handoffs.

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟯: 𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁

✸ PydanticAI → typed agents + dependencies  
✸ Deep Agents → planning + persistent context  
✸ Mastra → workflows + memory + tools

→ One agent can plan, execute, and recover from errors.

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟰: 𝗙𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁

✸ Claude Code → filesystem-based coding agent  
✸ just-bash → Bash + virtual filesystem  
✸ Vercel Sandbox → isolated code execution

→ File system + Bash roughly doubled the eval score.

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟱: 𝗥𝗲𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀

✸ Anthropic Skills → reusable agent instructions  
✸ Skills CLI → discover + install skills  
✸ Vercel Agent Skills → domain-specific skills

→ Reuse proven workflows instead of starting from scratch.

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟲: 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗙𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸

✸ Eve → filesystem-first agent framework  
✸ Workflow DevKit → durable execution  
✸ OpenTelemetry → tracing + observability
→ Turn files, tools, and skills into deployable agents.

And this is the architectural progression:

Big Prompt  
→ Multi-Agent System  
→ Stateful Agent  
→ File System + Bash  
→ Reusable Skills  
→ Production Runtime

𝗣𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿:

Sometimes better context, familiar tools, and a simple file system can outperform an elaborate multi-agent workflow. The trick is knowing when to add complexity and when to remove it.

I may benchmark LangGraph vs Google ADK vs PydanticAI vs Deep Agents vs Eve next, using Insurance Claims, Wind Turbine Maintenance, or Legal Contracts.
